population_note: Eight of 16 selected papers have locked eligible questions and bounded future-evidence audits. Do not compute cohort prevalence or Paper 3 skill from these rows.

rows.question: For automated repair proposals from the same repair bot, does attaching a natural-language explanation plus a concrete behavioral-difference example improve blinded reviewer acceptance or time-to-decision compared with a patch-only proposal, at matched patch correctness and review workload?
search_terms: patch explanations reviewer acceptance automated repair experiment 2020 2021 2022 2023
explainable patch review time acceptance program repair
Evaluating Explanations Software Patches LLM SSBSE 2023
rows.supported_dimension_scope: A 2023 primary study evaluated LLM-generated explanations for 30 machine-generated and human-written Defects4J patches with three independent reviewers. It measured explanation correctness, completeness, complexity and continuity, finding 84% correctness and 54% completeness for machine-generated patches in at least one of three runs. It did not manipulate patch-only versus explainable presentation or measure reviewer acceptance/time-to-decision, so it is partial progress on explanation quality only.

evidence.title: Evaluating Explanations for Software Patches Generated by Large Language Models
evidence.locator: PDF pp. 1-3 experimental design; pp. 4-5 results and threats
evidence.independence: Different author group from the 2019 source; uses ARJA-e/Defects4J patches and three independent reviewers.
evidence.observed_claim: For 30 bugs, GPT-3.5 explanations of machine-generated patches were correct in 84% and complete in 54% of cases in at least one of three runs. Evaluation was manual content assessment; there was no patch-only control and no adoption, decision-time or comprehension task outcome.

excluded_near_matches.reason: A 2022 study proposal targets human acceptance/rejection of APR security patches, but the bounded record describes planned methodology rather than an authenticated observed outcome.
2019 pre-cutoff observational study of merged patch explanations; it cannot be used as future evidence for the 2019 source cutoff or as a causal acceptance test.

rows.decision: The question remains direct-outcome unadjudicated. Future work should manipulate patch-only versus explainable presentation with blinded reviewers and record acceptance, understanding and time; explanation-quality scores alone do not validate the claimed integration benefit.
rows.limitations: The 2023 study's sample is 30 one-file Defects4J bugs and uses subjective manual ratings; exact acceptance effect remains unknown.

rows.question: On held-out DNN bug-fix instances, does a DNN-aware repair/localization intervention reduce incorrect or vulnerability-introducing patches relative to a code-only repair baseline while preserving verified bug-fix success?
search_terms: DNN automated repair regression vulnerability introduced patches DeepDiagnosis 2022
Repairing DNN Architecture Are We There Yet 2023 random baseline
DNN repair benchmark automated bug repair 2021 2022 2023
rows.supported_dimension_scope: DeepDiagnosis evaluates dynamic DNN fault detection/localization and actionable recommendations on 444 models, while a 2023 DNN-architecture repair study compares repair methods on real and mutated faulty models and reports random baselines comparable to or better than existing methods, with all methods failing on larger/complex models. These studies provide progress on diagnosis and performance repair, but do not run the frozen DNN-aware versus code-only comparison with verified regression/security outcomes.

evidence.title: DeepDiagnosis: Automatically Diagnosing Faults and Recommending Actionable Fixes in Deep Learning Programs
evidence.locator: PDF p. 1 abstract; pp. 9-10 related work/conclusion
evidence.independence: Different author group and tool; evaluates 53 real-world plus 391 curated models.
evidence.observed_claim: DeepDiagnosis outperforms listed fault-localization baselines and supplies actionable recommendations, but explicitly does not perform automated fixes; its future work includes automatic repair and additional bug types.

evidence.title: Repairing DNN Architecture: Are We There Yet?
evidence.locator: PDF pp. 3-5 benchmark construction; conclusion/abstract; RQs in section 4
evidence.independence: Different author group and benchmark; real and mutation-generated faulty DNN models.
evidence.observed_claim: Random search is comparable to or outperforms existing repair methods in some cases, and all tested techniques fail on larger and more complicated models. The endpoint is model-performance repair, not introduced-bug/security regression under the frozen comparison.

excluded_near_matches.reason: Java vulnerability repair study, not DNN application/framework repair; its low repair rates are a different object and cannot directly resolve the frozen DNN question.
A later DNN repair method/benchmark outside the fixed 2020-2025 window end as authenticated here; not counted without a verified in-window first-public date in this audit.

rows.decision: Retain as partial progress plus scope narrowing, not a direct resolution or contradiction. A decisive test needs project-disjoint DNN repair units, a code-only baseline, verified fix success, regression/security checks and independent seeds/models.
rows.limitations: The two follow-ups use different endpoints and intervention boundaries. Their positive/negative method comparisons are not causal evidence for avoiding vulnerability-introducing fixes.

rows.question: For exact metric sparsifiers of Zero Extension with s labels and crossing-number parameter k, is an exponent growing with s necessary in worst-case sparsifier size, or can an exponent independent of s suffice?
search_terms: metric sparsifier Zero Extension lower bound labels 2020 2021 2022
zero extension sparsifier lower bound 2023
Reidl Wahlström metric sparsifier lower bound

excluded_near_matches.reason: Same-team 2018 conference version of source upper bound, not a future answer.
2024 result lies outside 2019-2023 window and concerns a 0-Extension LP/Steiner-node integrality gap, not exact metric-sparsifier size.
A different metric vertex sparsifier quality/distortion lower-bound setting; not the source's exact size question, and first-public date not verified in this audit.

rows.decision: Keep direct formal answer unadjudicated. Forward-citation/theorem-definition tracing is more informative than generic sparsifier searches; no future theorem was authenticated here.

rows.question: Across held-out industrial software projects, does adding software artifacts to the CAM log-based test-alarm classifier improve independently verified cause-classification accuracy over log-only CAM at matched training budget?
search_terms: CAM test alarm software artifacts external projects followup
LogFaultFlagger CAM Ericsson comparison 2019
What Causes My Test Alarm CAM replication industrial dataset
rows.supported_dimension_scope: An independent 2019 team reimplemented log-only CAM on a different industrial dataset, finding 50% of product faults at K=15 and explicitly attributing poor transfer to skewed Ericsson data. This establishes a cross-company baseline component and motivates the scope restriction, but not a matched artifact-augmentation experiment or multiclass cause accuracy. Metrics across the 2017 and 2019 papers are not directly comparable.

evidence.title: Mining Historical Test Logs to Predict Bugs and Localize Faults in the Test Logs
evidence.date_scope: ICSE 2019 opening date is a latest-by public conference bound, not the authenticated first author-draft posting date; the exact first date is unknown but the work was public in-window.
evidence.locator: PDF pp. 1-2 CAM contrast; p. 6 Table I and Result 1; p. 8 Discussion
evidence.independence: Amar and Rigby at Concordia, using Ericsson data, distinct from Jiang et al.'s CAM team and Huawei data.
evidence.observed_claim: The independent authors reimplemented CAM on Ericsson failure logs and report 50% FaultsFound for product faults at K=15, with skewed environmental failures limiting majority-vote KNN. They altered the task to binary product-fault detection and fault-line localization. They did not add test scripts or other artifacts to CAM, did not evaluate held-out project-level multiclass cause accuracy, and did not report matched labeling/training budget.

excluded_near_matches.reason: The reported 50% product-fault recall and source CAM's 58.3%/65.8% multiclass accuracy differ in endpoint and datasets. They cannot be called a direct contradiction or a direct answer about extra artifacts.
Different multisource microservice diagnosis system and outside the fixed 2018-2022 window.

rows.decision: Do not claim CAM artifact augmentation succeeds or fails. The independent transfer failure changes the experiment priority: before adding artifacts, predeclare industrial project-level splits, class-imbalance handling and both multiclass accuracy and product-fault recall; then run artifact-on/off ablation if comparable data access exists.
rows.limitations: Independent cross-company evidence is one industrial dataset, with changed task/metric. The 2019 conference is date-verified, but earliest author-draft posting is not. No direct resolution.

coupled tasks bounded-degree tree compatibility graph 2018 2022

rows.question: At matched total CPU resources, does parallelized Badger generate higher worst-case resource-cost inputs than a standalone cost-guided fuzzer on held-out Java subjects within the same wall-clock budget?
search_terms: Badger parallel symbolic execution KelinciWCA fair comparison CPU worst case 2019 2020
Badger complexity analysis fuzzing symbolic execution follow up parallelize symbolic execution 2020 2021
HotFuzz Badger benchmark evaluation 2020 2021 worst case
rows.supported_dimension_scope: An independent team showed that a different, guided Java micro-fuzzer can produce and confirm algorithmic-complexity vulnerability witnesses; this strengthens the broad premise that cost-guided testing is empirically useful, not the causal/resource-fair advantage of Badger's hybrid architecture.

evidence.title: HotFuzz: Discovering Algorithmic Denial-of-Service Vulnerabilities Through Guided Micro-Fuzzing
evidence.locator: PDF p. 1 abstract; pp. 11-13 evaluation and Table II
evidence.independence: Different author group and separate Java library/JRE/STAC evaluation; method is HotFuzz, not Badger.
evidence.observed_claim: The authors evaluate guided micro-fuzzing over the JRE, STAC challenges and 100 popular Maven libraries; Table II reports AC witnesses and confirmed cases under SRI versus IVI seed strategies. This does not include matched-CPU Badger versus standalone KelinciWCA.

excluded_near_matches.reason: Same broad vulnerability-search domain but a different intervention and comparator; only its reference list cites Badger. Not direct resolution or a strict subcase of the frozen fair-resource comparison.
Review chapter of symbolic-execution applications, not a direct matched-resource Badger experiment.

rows.decision: The broad premise has independent support, while the source's fair-resource hybrid advantage remains untested in authenticated in-window evidence. Prioritize a low-cost feasibility audit of pinned Badger/KelinciWCA code and a paired matched-CPU experiment only if builds and cost metric can be reproduced.
rows.limitations: Bounded web search, not exhaustive citation tracing. No direct future result was authenticated. One positive trajectory dimension must not be treated as resolution, prevalence or forecast validation.

rows.question: For records with low single-query PDTP, can multiple selected queries to the same classifier raise membership-inference accuracy over a single direct-query baseline at a fixed query budget?
search_terms: differential training privacy PDTP multiple queries indirect membership inference attack 2018 2019 2020
label-only membership inference multiple perturbed queries 2020 2021 low PDTP
rows.supported_dimension_scope: Later work demonstrates the multiple-selected-query attack component: label-only inference from perturbed samples outperforms a one-label gap baseline on studied image classifiers. It does not stratify target records by the 2017 source's low PDTP or directly test their claimed safety, so it is partial progress only.

evidence.title: Label-Only Membership Inference Attacks
evidence.locator: PDF pp. 2-3, attack design and single-label gap baseline; pp. 5-7, Figure 2 and query-budget comparison
evidence.independence: Different authors from the 2017 DTP/PDTP source; own classifiers and experiments, but this is not a PDTP-stratified replication.
evidence.observed_claim: Multiple strategically perturbed label queries are used for membership inference. On the reported CIFAR-10 setup, 3-query rotation or (4d+1)-query translation attacks and larger-budget boundary attacks exceed the one-label gap baseline for some settings; the paper reports 3-4 percentage-point improvements at tuned small perturbations. No PDTP values or low-PDTP subgroup analysis are reported in the inspected PDF.

evidence.title: Sampling Attacks: Amplification of Membership Inference Attacks by Repeated Queries
evidence.date_scope: arXiv v1 only; PDF notes an earlier NeurIPS 2019 workshop version whose exact first date was not authenticated here
evidence.locator: PDF p. 1 version note/abstract; p. 6 Algorithm 1 and section 5
evidence.independence: Different author team; not a matched low-PDTP subgroup test.
evidence.observed_claim: Repeated perturbed-label queries are aggregated into attack features. Exact first publication may predate arXiv v1 via the stated 2019 workshop version; either date remains within the 2018-2022 window. This paper is not counted as a separate independent outcome unit for prevalence.

excluded_near_matches.reason: No PDTP measurement/stratification; a stronger attack against a general population cannot directly refute low-PDTP safety under the frozen source metric.

rows.decision: Track low-PDTP vulnerability as still unadjudicated. A decisive affordable experiment would compute PDTP per record on a pinned classifier, then compare single-query and prespecified multiple-query attacks at record level with independent model/data units and query budgets.
rows.limitations: Partial progress, not direct resolution or a proven privacy failure for low-PDTP records. The 2021 ICML PDF is used with its verified earlier 2020 arXiv v1 date; the second paper's workshop precedence requires version pinning before citing it as earliest evidence.

search_terms: TraceDiff deployed classroom evaluation real course programming feedback 2018 2019 2020
TraceDiff course evaluation students 2018 2019

excluded_near_matches.reason: A different autograding feedback system reports classroom deployment, not TraceDiff versus Python Tutor on matched iterative tasks.

analysis_gate: No Paper 3 evaluation: six audited questions and zero directly adjudicated binary outcomes provide no valid class contrast or temporal test.
